title: The Chair Is Adjustable: Find Your Starting Point in a Sit-to-Stand
subtitle: A chair rise is not a score to beat. Change the support, setup or pace so the movement meets you where you are—and build from there.
imageAlt: Two friends practice standing up from sturdy chairs in a bright living room; one uses their hands for support while the other rises without them.
imageConcept: A warm, natural-light living room with two friends side by side, each using a sturdy chair. One person presses lightly through their hands as they rise; the other stands without hand support. Both look focused and comfortable, making different starting points visible without presenting one as the winner.
body: A movement with more than one starting line

Standing up from a chair is so familiar that it can be easy to mistake it for a test: rise without using your hands, repeat as quickly as possible, count the result. But the useful question is not whether you can do the movement in one prescribed way. It is how to make the movement controlled and appropriate for you today. A chair rise works the muscles of the thighs and buttocks, and the CDC’s STEADI handout recommends beginning with hand support, using the hands less as strength improves, and controlling the return to sitting [1]. That is a progression, not a pass-or-fail rule.

The same movement can look different from person to person. One person may press from the armrests; another may use fingertips on a stable support; a third may rise without their hands. Those versions can share a purpose without requiring identical ability, confidence or range of motion. Treat the chair as adjustable equipment: its height, position and your support all shape the task.
Set the room up before you move

Choose a sturdy, non-wheeled chair that will not slide or fold, with a seat height that lets you sit and stand with control. Place it on a level surface and, if it can be done safely, against a wall so it is less likely to shift. Clear nearby clutter, secure loose rugs and make sure the route around the chair is open. Wear footwear that feels secure. If you need hand support, decide where it will come from before beginning; a stable counter or fixed rail may be safer than a light chair that could move when pressed.

Sit near the front of the seat, with your feet planted comfortably beneath or slightly behind your knees. The exact position is personal: the CDC compendium describes changing chair position and foot placement, along with hand support and lowering control, as ways programs vary sit-to-stand difficulty [2]. You do not need to force a particular posture or copy a diagram precisely. Choose a setup in which you can lean forward enough to begin rising while keeping your balance and feeling secure.
The basic rise: steady, not hurried

Start seated, with your back supported if that is more comfortable. Let your feet rest flat where possible. If you are using your hands, place them on the chair’s armrests or another support you have already checked for stability. Lean your torso forward a little, bring your weight over your feet, and press through your feet and, if needed, your hands to stand. Pause once upright. Then bend at the hips and knees and lower yourself back to the seat slowly enough to stay in control.

There is no need to make the rise explosive or to drop into the chair. The descent is part of the movement, not an afterthought; the CDC handout specifically advises controlling it [1]. Keep your breathing comfortable rather than holding it. If you need several small adjustments to get into position, take them before starting. A smooth repetition may include hand assistance. The practical target is a movement you can repeat without rushing, wobbling or relying on momentum to get through it.
Adjust the challenge before adding more

If the movement feels difficult, first make it easier rather than pushing through. Use the armrests or a stable support, choose a higher seat if one is available and safe, or do fewer repetitions. The CDC advises starting with fewer repetitions if its suggested amount is too challenging [1]. You can also pause between repetitions or practice the controlled lowering phase with support. A shorter range of movement may be a reasonable starting point if standing all the way feels uncomfortable, but do not force a range that causes pain or loss of control.

If the movement feels comfortable and steady, change only one element at a time. You might use a little less hand pressure, choose a slightly lower seat, or add one repetition while keeping the rest of the setup the same. The CDC compendium lists variations including hand support, chair position, foot position, resistance and control of the lowering phase; it also emphasizes tailoring exercises to participants’ abilities [2]. That menu is not a requirement to make every version harder. It is a reminder that challenge has several dials.

A useful progression can be modest: today you stand using both hands; later you use one hand; eventually you may be comfortable with less support. Or your progression may be keeping the same hand support while making the descent more controlled. Record the version you chose—chair height, support, repetitions and any rest—so you can compare like with like. If the next attempt feels less steady, return to the easier version. That is adjustment, not failure.

Avoid turning a practice set into a timed contest. Speed can obscure whether the movement is controlled, and a repetition count does not tell you whether your setup is suitable. Stop if you feel pain, dizziness, unusual shortness of breath or unsteadiness; sit safely and seek appropriate professional guidance if symptoms persist or concern you. If you have a condition, recent injury or specific restrictions, ask a clinician or physical therapist how to adapt the movement before making it more challenging. General instructions cannot account for every person’s circumstances.
One movement belongs in a larger picture

Chair rises can be a practical way to rehearse a familiar movement while strengthening the lower body, but they are not a complete fitness plan or a promise of a particular outcome. A scoping review of sit-to-stand interventions found only six eligible studies among 3,041 papers, with differences in program length and frequency and limitations in study rigor that constrained broad conclusions [3]. That makes it sensible to value the movement without claiming it will produce the same result for everyone.

Strength is one part of physical activity. A fuller routine may also include aerobic activity, balance work and flexibility, adapted to a person’s abilities and needs. The important distinction is between a useful exercise and a universal prescription. If chair rises fit your life and feel appropriate, they can be one option among many. If they do not, another supported strength exercise may be a better place to begin. The right starting point is the one that lets you practice with control and return to it safely.
Choose a version you can repeat

For a first practice, set aside a few unhurried minutes and use a sturdy chair on a clear, level floor. Decide in advance whether you will use the armrests or another stable support. Try one controlled rise and return, then pause and notice: Did the chair stay put? Could you lower yourself smoothly? Did the setup feel secure? If not, adjust the support or seat before deciding whether to try again. Begin with a small number of repetitions that leaves you feeling in control, rather than trying to prove what you can manage.

When you practice with someone else, agree that each person can choose a different version and stop without explanation. One person’s next step might be less hand pressure; another’s might be simply repeating the same comfortable setup another time. Write down the version that worked and revisit it when you are ready. A shared practice does not require matching bodies, pace or milestones. The point is to build a repeatable movement around the person doing it.
